Lecture 19: The Operational Amplifier Abstraction
summary: Introduces the operational amplifier as an abstraction with an ideal circuit model (huge gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance) and shows its unreliable open-loop gain on a scope. A non-inverting amplifier is then analyzed to show that negative feedback makes the gain depend only on resistor ratios, with anti-lock brakes as an analogy.

title: Lecture 22: Energy and Power
summary: After wrapping up the op amp oscillator by using it as a clock that discretizes time, the lecture turns to energy and power: it derives static power for a resistive path and shows that charging and discharging a capacitor costs CV^2 per cycle. These combine into static plus CV^2f dynamic power for an inverter, demonstrated with a power meter and a chip-scale estimate.

summary: A guest lecturer recasts the RC response in terms of state, splitting it into zero-state and zero-input parts, then uses capacitor charge storage to build a memory cell. The cell is refined from a DRAM-style switch and capacitor into buffered and feedback-based static memory, closing with a small decoded four-bit memory.

title: Lecture 23: Energy, CMOS
summary: Shows that the resistive-load NMOS inverter would make a 100-million-gate chip dissipate an absurd static power, then motivates and introduces the PFET and the CMOS inverter, which removes the supply-to-ground path and speeds up rising edges. Closes with CV^2f scaling, supply reduction, clock gating, leakage, and a demo that overheats a CMOS inverter.
